keyTakeaways: 52 Halloween words fall into six groups: creatures, objects, customs, colours, sounds and atmosphere adjectives.
Of 48 two-word Halloween phrases here, 12 are common set phrases such as spooky season and 36 are original pairs such as lantern weather.
Jack-o'-lantern first named a marsh light in the 1660s; the carved-pumpkin sense is recorded from 1834.
In a 64-student study, words for physically similar things caused 36 mix-ups against 1 for unrelated words, so keep pumpkin and gourd in separate lessons.
48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, which is why two-word phrases beat long lines on a card.

faqs.question: What is a good two-word Halloween phrase for a caption?
faqs.answer: Pick a pair that names a feeling rather than an object, such as lantern weather, hush hour or candy audit. Those three are among the 36 original pairs on this page; spooky season and pumpkin patch work too, but they are common set phrases thousands of other captions already use.

faqs.question: What does the witching hour mean?
faqs.answer: It means midnight, the hour when witches and other supernatural beings were thought to be active, and loosely any late hour when odd things happen. Wiktionary credits Hamlet, written around 1599 to 1602, with popularising it through the line about the witching time of night.

faqs.question: Where does the word jack-o'-lantern come from?
faqs.answer: Wiktionary traces it to a night watchman who carried a lantern. From the 1660s it named the flickering marsh light of folklore, mostly in East Anglia, and the carved-pumpkin sense is first recorded in 1834.

faqs.question: Is eerie the same as creepy?
faqs.answer: Not quite. Eerie describes a place or a silence that feels wrong, while creepy describes something, often a person, that makes your skin crawl; Wiktionary defines creepy by that crawling sensation.

faqs.question: What is guising?
faqs.answer: Guising is a historical custom of going out in disguise, often playing pranks, according to Wiktionary. Souling, another old practice, meant giving and receiving soul cakes on All Souls' Day, 2 November.

faqs.question: Which Halloween idiom means very frightened?
faqs.answer: Scared stiff, which Wiktionary records from the 1890s, means too frightened to move. Make your blood run cold means to horrify, and bloodcurdling is the matching adjective.

faqs.question: How many Halloween words should I teach in one ESL lesson?
faqs.answer: No study has tested an ideal number for Halloween. Lázaro Ibarrola and Hidalgo Gordo used sets of 10 and Ishii used sets of 6; the clearer lesson from both is to mix word types and keep look-alikes such as pumpkin and gourd in separate lessons.

faqs.question: What are long Halloween words for crosswords?
faqs.answer: Poltergeist has 11 letters, and jack-o'-lantern and will-o'-the-wisp each have 12 once the hyphens and apostrophes are dropped. Grimalkin and scarecrow give you 9, eldritch and cauldron 8.

faqs.question: Is it skeleton in the closet or skeleton in the cupboard?
faqs.answer: Both mean a shameful secret. Wiktionary labels skeleton in the closet as US and skeleton in the cupboard as UK, so pick the one that matches your reader.

faqs.question: Is spooky season an original phrase?
faqs.answer: No. Spooky season is one of the 12 common set phrases on this page, alongside haunted house and pumpkin patch; the 36 pairs marked original were written for this page instead of being copied from any list.

faqs.question: Can I send one Halloween word to one person on a pumpkin?
faqs.answer: Yes. SubhSandesh's Halloween card asks for a word to carve on its jack-o'-lantern, and the recipient carves until the candle lights and the word glows. It is a one-person greeting page with partner, bestie, family and kids modes, not a classroom or party tool.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Phrases and Words: 52 Terms, 48 Pairs and 14 Idioms

Halloween phrases are the set expressions, two-word pairings and idioms that carry the season's mood, and the most usable are under three words. Short matters: 48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, and each page averages 11.1 views, so a line gets reread on a small screen. Below are 52 Halloween words with one-line definitions, 48 two-word phrases (12 labelled common, 36 written here) and 14 idioms, with dictionary-checked origins where one exists.

## What is the difference between a Halloween word, a phrase and an idiom?

A Halloween word is a single term tied to 31 October, such as banshee or guising. A phrase is two or more words used together, like "haunted house"; an idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words, like "skeleton in the closet" for a shameful secret.

The name itself is a Scots clipping of Allhalloweven, the night before All Hallows' Day on 1 November. Origins below come from Wiktionary entries such as [jack-o'-lantern](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/jack-o%27-lantern), and no origin is guessed.

## Halloween words: 52 terms in 6 groups, with plain definitions

Six groups, one plain line each, for a reader meeting the word cold.

### 1. Creatures (10)

- **Banshee**: a female spirit whose wail warns of a death; from Irish, in English since 1771.
- **Poltergeist**: an unseen ghost that moves objects; German poltern (rumble) plus Geist (ghost).
- **Wraith**: a ghost seen just after a death; first recorded in 1513, in an Aeneid translation.
- **Ghoul**: a demon said to feed on corpses; from Arabic, via French.
- **Goblin**: a small, mischievous being; reached English through Norman French.
- **Zombie**: a body animated without a will; ultimately from a Bantu language.
- **Hag**: a witch or crone; Old English hægtesse.
- **Grimalkin**: an old cat; grey plus malkin.
- **Spook**: a ghost; borrowed from Dutch.
- **Familiar**: a witch's animal helper.

### 2. Objects and food (9)

- **Jack-o'-lantern**: a carved, candlelit pumpkin; once a night watchman with a lantern, the pumpkin sense dates from 1834.
- **Gourd**: a hard-shelled fruit related to the pumpkin; from Latin cucurbita.
- **Cauldron**: a large cooking pot.
- **Broomstick**: a broom's handle, the witch's transport.
- **Candy corn**: striped yellow, orange and white sweets shaped like maize kernels.
- **Cobweb**: an old, dusty spider web.
- **Scarecrow**: a straw figure guarding crops; it displaced older names like bogle.
- **Lantern**: a portable, enclosed light.
- **Tombstone**: a grave marker.

### 3. Customs (8)

- **Guising**: a historical custom of going out in disguise, often with pranks.
- **Souling**: giving and receiving soul cakes on All Souls' Day.
- **Trick-or-treating**: going door to door in costume for sweets.
- **Apple bobbing**: catching floating apples with your teeth.
- **Wake**: a watch kept over the dead.
- **Séance**: a gathering meant to contact spirits.
- **Haunt**: to visit a place often; related to home.
- **Will-o'-the-wisp**: a marsh light that folklore says lures travellers astray.

### 4. Colours (7)

- **Pumpkin orange**: the season's lead colour.
- **Midnight black**: cats, bats and silhouettes.
- **Bruise purple**: witch hats and dusk.
- **Bone white**: skeletons and candles.
- **Slime green**: potions and monster skin.
- **Candle gold**: the glow inside a jack-o'-lantern.
- **Ash grey**: fog and old stone.

### 5. Sounds (8)

- **Creak**: a slow groan from a door or stair.
- **Cackle**: a sharp, broken laugh.
- **Howl**: a long, rising cry.
- **Rattle**: quick knocking, like loose bones.
- **Shriek**: a sudden, high scream.
- **Moan**: a low sound of pain.
- **Hiss**: a long "sss" from a cat.
- **Thud**: a heavy, dull landing.

### 6. Atmosphere adjectives (10)

- **Eerie**: strange in a way that unsettles; in Scots it can also mean frightened.
- **Creepy**: like things crawling on your skin; from creep.
- **Eldritch**: weird and unearthly; from older elritch, origin uncertain.
- **Macabre**: dwelling on death; from French, origin uncertain.
- **Uncanny**: familiar and wrong at once.
- **Ghastly**: deathly pale, or awful.
- **Spectral**: ghost-like.
- **Gothic**: gloomy, ornate and old.
- **Bloodcurdling**: frightening enough to chill the blood.
- **Spooky**: suggestive of ghosts; built on spook.

Eerie and creepy are not twins. Eerie is a place or silence that feels wrong; creepy is something, often someone, that makes your skin crawl.

## Halloween phrases 2 words: 48 pairs, common and original

Two words fit a caption, a card or a carved pumpkin. The first 12 are common set phrases; the other 36 are our own.

### 7. Common set phrases (12)

- spooky season
- haunted house
- pumpkin patch
- costume party
- ghost story
- jump scare
- full moon
- black cat
- corn maze
- hay ride
- sugar rush
- candy haul

### 8. Original cosy pairs (12)

- lantern weather
- cider dusk
- cobweb cardigan
- porchlight season
- blanket o'clock
- gourd gallery
- ember evening
- toffee twilight
- crunch season
- sweater fog
- spiced dark
- candle curfew

### 9. Original eerie pairs (12)

- hush hour
- attic static
- marrow chill
- crypt quiet
- moth light
- stairwell echo
- bone weather
- shadow tenant
- mirror lag
- cellar breath
- raven hours
- unlit porch

### 10. Original funny pairs (12)

- candy audit
- wrapper evidence
- costume regret
- sugar hangover
- fang floss
- broom parking
- ghost mode
- cape traffic
- treat inflation
- doorbell marathon
- wig casualty
- pillowcase haul

"Original" means not copied from any list, not that nobody has ever typed the pair. Search one before printing it on merchandise.

## 14 Halloween idioms and set phrases, with what they mean

These carry a Halloween flavour all year. Origins appear only where a dictionary gives one.

### 11. Idioms with a checked origin (6)

- **Witching hour**: midnight; popularised by "the witching time of night" in Hamlet, written around 1599 to 1602, per [Wiktionary](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/witching_hour).
- **Scared stiff**: too frightened to move; recorded from the 1890s.
- **Graveyard shift**: work from midnight to 8 a.m.; the dictionary ties it to silent nights and graveyards, not the buried-alive bell tale.
- **Skeleton in the closet**: a shameful secret; US, while the UK says skeleton in the cupboard.
- **Will-o'-the-wisp**: figuratively, a goal you keep chasing but never reach.
- **Jack-o'-lantern**: from the 1660s, mainly in East Anglia, the marsh light itself.

### 12. Idioms by meaning (8)

- **Not a ghost of a chance**: no chance at all.
- **Give up the ghost**: to die, or for a machine to stop working.
- **Ghost town**: a deserted place.
- **Over my dead body**: a flat refusal.
- **Dig your own grave**: to cause your own downfall.
- **Make your blood run cold**: to horrify.
- **Witch hunt**: a campaign against people for their views.
- **Skeleton crew**: the fewest staff who can keep things running.

## Halloween word types compared: example, meaning and best use

This table compares five word types by what each does best. It describes language only; SubhSandesh holds no Halloween usage figures.

| Word type | Example | Meaning | Best use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Creature noun | banshee (7 letters) | a wailing spirit that warns of death | storytelling, crossword fill |
| Atmosphere adjective | eldritch (8 letters) | weird and unearthly | descriptive writing, B2+ learners |
| Custom term | souling (7 letters) | giving soul cakes on All Souls' Day | history lessons, quizzes |
| Two-word phrase | candle curfew (2 words) | original cosy pairing | captions, a carved pumpkin word |
| Idiom | scared stiff (from the 1890s) | too frightened to move | conversation practice |

Nouns and pairs go on things; idioms only work inside a sentence.

## Halloween vocabulary for teachers and word games: what two studies found

A Halloween lesson is a themed word set, and the research is more cautious than most worksheets. Lázaro Ibarrola and Hidalgo Gordo taught 57 Spanish secondary students 10 related and 10 unrelated words, and [unrelated sets were retained better](https://digibug.ugr.es/handle/10481/53761): 10 beginners scored full marks on unrelated words, 5 on related ones, in a short-term test.

Ishii's study of 64 Japanese university students found [words for physically similar things caused the most confusion](https://www.castledown.com/journals/vli/article/view/vli.v02.1.ishii): 36 mix-ups, against 13 for same-category words and 1 for unrelated ones. Ishii also cites Tinkham's finding that themes mixing parts of speech (frog, hop, slimy, pond) help.

For a Halloween lesson, that suggests three rules to follow:

- Mix nouns, verbs and adjectives in one set: ghost, haunt, eerie, creak.
- Keep round, orange look-alikes apart: pumpkin, gourd and lantern in different lessons.
- Teach idioms in a sentence, never as a bare list.

Crossword and word-game setters need lengths, not definitions. Counted without hyphens or apostrophes, the best fills are:

- 5 letters: GOURD, GHOUL, SPOOK
- 6 letters: WRAITH, CACKLE, GOBLIN
- 7 letters: BANSHEE, SOULING, MACABRE
- 8 letters: ELDRITCH, CAULDRON, SPECTRAL
- 9 letters: GRIMALKIN, SCARECROW
- 11 letters: POLTERGEIST
- 12 letters: JACKOLANTERN, WILLOTHEWISP

## Putting one Halloween word on a pumpkin for one person

A word list is for a class, but one word can be for one person. The [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) asks for a word to carve on its pumpkin, and the recipient carves until it glows, so "lantern weather" or plain "boo" has a home. Making one takes roughly 5 minutes; it holds six photos at most and offers partner, bestie, family and kids modes.

This is a greeting for one recipient, not a classroom tool or party invitation. The [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note (60 seconds maximum) and room for 12 photos, with your initials lit on a pumpkin instead of a carved word. Platform-wide, 90.9% of started pages get published and shared.

## When a Halloween word list is the wrong tool

For a class of 30, a printed glossary and a crossword beat any link, and both Halloween pages have an English-only interface. Save idioms like "give up the ghost" for later lessons, since their words do not add up to their meaning.

Common phrases have limits too. "Spooky season" is everywhere, so it adds nothing to a card for one person; choose one of the 36 original pairs, or two words only you two would get.

## Sources

- Lázaro Ibarrola and Hidalgo Gordo (2015), [Should EFL Teachers Present Vocabulary in Semantically Related Sets?](https://digibug.ugr.es/handle/10481/53761), Porta Linguarum 23.
- Ishii (2013), [Reexamining semantic clustering](https://www.castledown.com/journals/vli/article/view/vli.v02.1.ishii), Vocabulary Learning and Instruction 2(1).
- Wiktionary, [jack-o'-lantern](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/jack-o%27-lantern) and [witching hour](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/witching_hour), checked 13 October 2026.

sources.stat: Lázaro Ibarrola & Hidalgo Gordo, 'Should EFL Teachers Present Vocabulary in Semantically Related Sets?', Porta Linguarum 23: 25-40 (Universidad de Granada), doi:10.30827/Digibug.53761. Two intact classes of Spanish secondary EFL learners (33 + 24 = 57) learned 10 unrelated and 10 semantically related (city) words; unrelated sets were retained better in both groups; in the beginner group 10 learners scored full marks on the unrelated set vs 5 on the related set. No delayed post-test (authors call results preliminary). Full text read (PDF).

Ishii, 'Reexamining semantic clustering: Insight from memory models', Vocabulary Learning and Instruction 2(1), doi:10.7820/vli.v02.1.ishii, open access (CC BY-NC-ND, cited not reproduced). 64 Japanese first/second-year students at a Tokyo university learned nonwords paired with meanings in unrelated, semantically related and physically related (round / long-thin / rectangular) sets of 6; semantic vs unrelated not significantly different, physically related significantly lower on both tests; within-set confusions in Test 2: 1 unrelated, 13 semantic, 36 physical. Reports Tinkham (1997): thematic clustering across parts of speech (frog, hop, slimy, pond) facilitative. Full text read (PDF).

Wiktionary 'jack-o'-lantern': originally a night watchman who carried a lantern; first attested for ignis fatuus in the 1660s, mostly in East Anglia, also SW England; carved-pumpkin sense first attested 1834. Sister entries read the same session (13 Oct 2026): Halloween (Scots shortening of Allhalloweven), banshee (entered English 1771), wraith (first attested 1513, Aeneid translation), poltergeist, ghoul, goblin, zombie, hag, grimalkin, spook, gourd, scarecrow, guising, souling, haunt, eerie, creepy, eldritch, macabre, will o' the wisp (figurative sense), scared stiff (from 1890s), graveyard shift, skeleton in the closet (US) / cupboard (UK), candy corn.

Wiktionary 'witching hour': midnight, when witches and other supernatural beings were thought to be active; the 'midnight' sense popularised by 'the witching time of night' in Hamlet (written c. 1599–1602, published 1603).

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a reason to cite this over the five pages measured (Cambridge.es phrasal verbs, Educators Technology quotes, Proofed 2016, EnglishPath, Atlas Language School): none defines a grouped Halloween glossary, none offers two-word phrases or labels common versus original, Atlas gives origins with no source, and none tells teachers how to group the words using research (Lázaro Ibarrola 2015, Ishii 2013). The first-party numbers are site-wide, not Halloween data, the idiom section covers table-stakes ground the ESL sites already own, and the domain is far weaker than the incumbents, so expect months, not weeks.
